nameStory: The Forest Disc gets its name from its perfectly round, flattened shell that looks just like a tiny natural coin or disc. The 'forest' part tells you exactly where to look – this little snail calls the woodland floor its home, unlike its cousins who might prefer more open areas.
description: The Forest Disc is a tiny land snail with a remarkably flat, coin-shaped shell that's almost perfectly round when viewed from above. This diminutive mollusk rarely grows larger than a pencil eraser, typically measuring just 3-6 millimeters across. Its low-profile shell has multiple whorls (spiral chambers) that coil tightly together, creating that distinctive disc-like appearance. You'll need to look closely to spot these little creatures, as they're masters of blending in with leaf litter and forest debris.

idTips.label: Disc-shaped shell
idTips.description: The shell is remarkably flat and perfectly round, like a tiny brown coin that's been slightly domed – you can actually balance it on your fingertip like a miniature frisbee

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Smaller than a pencil eraser at just 3-6mm across – you'll need good lighting or a magnifying glass to see the intricate spiral pattern clearly

idTips.label: Tightly coiled whorls
idTips.description: The shell's spiral chambers are wound very tightly together, creating distinct ridges you can feel with your fingernail if you're gentle

idTips.label: Brownish coloration
idTips.description: The shell ranges from light tan to rich brown, often with a slightly glossy surface that catches light when fresh and clean

idTips.label: Translucent when backlit
idTips.description: Hold the shell up to bright light and you can see through it slightly, revealing the internal spiral structure like looking through frosted glass

habitat: Forest Disc snails live in mature deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly favoring areas with rich, moist leaf litter and decaying logs. You'll find them most often in maple-beech forests and areas with good overhead canopy that keeps the forest floor consistently damp. They prefer spots where fallen leaves have been decomposing for a while, creating that soft, spongy layer of humus that retains moisture.

seasonality.spring: Active and easiest to find as they emerge from winter hiding spots. Look for them crawling on damp leaves after spring rains when temperatures warm above 50°F.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid periods and after rainstorms. They retreat deep into leaf litter during dry spells, so check under logs and in consistently moist microsites.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek winter shelter. Fresh shells are often easiest to spot on newly fallen leaves before they get buried.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep in leaf litter, under logs, or in soil crevices. You're more likely to find empty shells on the surface than living snails during cold months.

funFact: Despite being smaller than your pinky nail, Forest Disc snails can live for 2-3 years and survive being completely frozen solid during New England winters – they produce a natural antifreeze in their bodies that prevents ice crystals from forming in their cells!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Angular Disc, but the Forest Disc has a more perfectly round shell while the Angular Disc has a slightly polygonal, angular outline. Memory trick: 'Forest is round like a full moon, Angular has angles like its name suggests.'
contextualKnowledge: Forest Disc snails are incredibly rare to observe in New England – with only 3 recorded sightings, finding one would be like discovering a tiny treasure. They're part of a group called 'micromollusks' that require specialized techniques to study, which is why they're so rarely documented despite potentially being more common than records suggest.
compareHints: The Forest Disc differs from its close relative the Angular Disc by having a more perfectly circular shell outline and typically slightly smaller size. While Angular Discs have subtle flat edges that give them a polygonal appearance, Forest Discs maintain that perfect coin-like roundness. Both species prefer similar forest habitats, but Forest Discs seem to favor deeper, more mature forest settings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Angular Disc differs from its close relative the Forest Disc by having more pronounced angular ridges spiraling around its shell, while the Forest Disc has a smoother, more rounded appearance.
